extracted.intended_audience: researchers applying for grant funding (graduate students, postdocs, early-career and new team leaders)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, general-audience guidance on why grant applications are rejected and how to revise or prepare proposals to get funded. Focuses on matching calls, eligibility, team and track record, structure, clarity, timing, submission rules, and getting feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project fits the scope of the call
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure your project exactly matches the specific criteria outlined in the funder's call for proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding bodies have very specific criteria; do NOT assume a great idea or strong record overrides scope mismatches. If uncertain, consult your institution’s grant support team or senior colleagues who have applied to that exact grant. You can also 'spin' or tailor the same project to different funders by changing emphasis (e.g., reframe medically-relevant work as an animal study or clinical trial for NHMRC versus basic research for ARC). Search databases (e.g., SPIN) or consider industry funding if you can't find a fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meet eligibility criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm you satisfy all eligibility requirements (career stage, institution type, location, time-since-PhD, etc.) before applying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications that fail eligibility are often disqualified automatically and notifications may come months later. Eligibility can be very specific (e.g., postdoc grants requiring applicants within a certain number of years since PhD). Many funders now allow explanations for career interruptions (parental leave, lab changes, illness) — use those sections and check with institutional support if unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient and appropriate track record
rubrics_metrics.description: Your publication, award, and prior-funding record should meet the expectations for the grant and be presented relative to opportunities you've had.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers compare applicants and may expect more publications/awards for senior grants. Many calls allow discussion of track record relative to opportunity. For proposed methods you haven't used, include preliminary data or add collaborators who provide required expertise. Demonstrating prior use of proposed methodologies strengthens credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team composition must make sense and show real contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemble a realistic project team whose roles and contributions align with the work — avoid token or name-only collaborators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For project grants, include core personnel who will actually contribute (e.g., 3–4 individuals plus staff). Reviewers will notice if a high-profile name is only there for recognition without real input. Use collaborators to fill technical gaps rather than just boosting prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate enough time to prepare the proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Give yourself substantial lead time — proposal preparation can take many months up to a full year depending on scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant writing is time-consuming: idea development, collaborators, preliminary data, budgets, literature reading, and multiple drafts. Set specific hard deadlines well before submission, delegate tasks, solicit early feedback, and treat time invested as an investment in your research career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct structure and clear summary up front
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the funder’s required structure or, if none provided, include a clear, impactful summary/abstract with aims, objectives, intended impacts, and a project outline at the start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many grants have strict structure/formatting rules — use them. If structure is unspecified, create a concise first page with project scope, aims, objectives, and impacts. Obtain examples of winning applications from institutional support. Consider using graphical abstracts or video abstracts where allowed (noting regional norms: large graphical abstracts common in Japan; ARC often expects a figure on the first page) to catch reviewers' attention — but always check guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the proposal simple, clear, and appropriately scoped
rubrics_metrics.description: Write concisely for a general-science audience, avoid jargon, focus on big-picture objectives, and propose only work that can reasonably be completed within the grant timeframe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers may not be experts in your narrow field and have limited attention; dense jargon or over-detailed minutiae will lose them. 'Less is more' applies to prose and project scope. Do not be over-ambitious — include experiments you can realistically finish in the grant period. Have non-specialist readers test clarity; excessive complexity or unclear writing invites negative reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit correctly and follow formatting rules exactly
rubrics_metrics.description: Adhere meticulously to all formatting, font, margin, figure, and submission-method requirements of the funder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small formatting errors (wrong font size, margins, figure numbering) can cause immediate disqualification — e.g., an application was rejected for using Calibri instead of Arial. Verify submission channels (online portal, institutional submission, email) and re-read guidelines repeatedly before final submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain broad and early feedback from colleagues and non-specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Get input from supervisors, senior researchers in and outside your field, and even non-scientists to ensure clarity and identify weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit feedback early and often. A senior researcher outside your field can highlight where the application fails to communicate to a general science audience. Removing jargon and improving readability may come from non-expert reviewers. Use colleagues to check structure, content, and compliance with guidelines.
